extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; general early-18th-century literate public; students of literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Annotated/collected Spectator essays and letters presenting literary criticism, moral commentary and contemporary correspondence (Addison & Steele), aimed at informing and instructing a broad reading public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (Aristotle)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The Fable ought to be dramatically constructed, like that of Tragedy, and that it should have for its Subject one entire and perfect action, having a beginning, a middle, and an end” (Aristotle, Poetics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's rule is quoted and discussed as a formal requirement for narrative construction: the epic/poem should form a complete whole (like an animal), distinct from history which treats many events over time. Emphasis on beginning, middle, end; unity is a key evaluative standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic vs Tragedy: parts and magnitude
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic Poetry 'agrees so far with Tragic as it is an imitation of great characters and actions' and Aristotle 'ranked a perfect tragedy above a perfect epic; for, he said, all the parts of the Epic poem are to be found in Tragedy, not all those of Tragedy in the Epic poem.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to judge relative merits: tragedy is held (by Aristotle's account) to achieve a tighter unity and completeness of parts; critics invoke this when comparing epic poets (e.g., Milton) with classical models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject should be a single person in heroic/epic poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Gildon's criticism: 'all the heroic poems of the ancients mentions some one person as the subject of their poem... But Milton begins his poem of things, and not of men.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implied standard for a heroic/epic poem: center the narrative on one principal person (hero) rather than a diffuse 'poem of things.' Deviation from this is taken as a defect by some critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic event should be prosperous
rubrics_metrics.description: Dryden: 'His Design is the Losing of our Happiness; his Event is not prosperous, like that of all other Epique Works.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden treats a successful, prosperous outcome as characteristic of 'epique' works; an epic whose event is not prosperous may be criticized for not fitting the heroic/epic norm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence and prominence of human characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Dryden's observation: 'His Heavenly Machines are many, and his Human Persons are but two.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics expect epics to feature a rich cast of human persons; an over-reliance on divine machinery and too few developed human characters is presented as a shortcoming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to Aristotelian critical rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapin (via Rymer): 'There is no arriving at Perfection but by these Rules, and they certainly go astray that take a different course.... And if a Poem made by these Rules fails of success, the fault lies not in the Art, but in the Artist.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A prescriptive standard: strict conformity to the rules of Aristotle (as interpreted by later critical authorities) is presented as the path to perfection; departures are treated as culpable or requiring justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and elevation of thought (classical imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dryden praises Milton: 'his Thoughts are elevated, his Words sounding, and that no Man has so happily copy'd the manner of Homer; or so copiously translated his Grecisms and the Latin Elegancies of Virgil.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Values elevated intellectual content and resonant language, and positive engagement with/classical imitation of Homer and Virgil. Also warns of long 'flats of thought' — moments where imagination flags for many lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verse form suitability (rhyme vs blank verse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dryden on Milton's blank verse: 'Neither will I justify Milton for his Blank Verse... his own particular Reason is plainly this, that Rhime was not his Talent; he had neither the Ease of doing it, nor the Graces of it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion focuses on appropriateness of metrical and rhyming choices to the poet's talent and to genre conventions; blank verse may be excused where rhyme is not a poet's strength, but departures from norms invite scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral responsibility / avoidance of deliberate advancement of vice
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele's moral criticism: 'a deliberate advancing of Vice, with all the Wit in the World, is as ill an Action as any that comes before the Magistrate... an Audience should rise against such a Scene, as throws down the Reputation of any thing which the Consideration of Religion or Decency should preserve from Contempt.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that deliberately promote or glamorize vice, insult religion, or undermine decency are condemnable regardless of literary skill; critics and audiences should reject such representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character plausibility and natural representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Steele's objection to the Chaplain and Sir Roger: their portrayals are 'trivial, senseless, and unnatural' and 'Monsters of the Poets own forming; the Sentiments in both of them are such as do not arise' from their education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters should be believable and arise naturally from their background and education; unnatural, implausible characterizations (especially of reputable or sacred roles) are a moral and artistic failing.
